notes: ⚠️ THE PROPERTY THAT MATTERS IS MODEL-INDEPENDENCE, not freshness alone. Three mechanisms produce fresh reads; only this one does so without the caching model being decided first. `io()` is the Cache Components primitive and the documentation prefers it — but it resolves immediately when Cache Components is off, so a route built on it would go SILENTLY STALE if that flag were ever turned off. A freshness contract that breaks quietly when an unrelated configuration changes is the same shape of defect as the build-time freeze it is meant to fix. ⚠️ `connection()` has a real cost, stated rather than buried: the documentation says it stays suspended until a full user navigation reaches the server, so it also blocks prefetches. `io()` does not. That is a genuine trade against model-independence and belongs in the decision.

notes: ⚠️ THIS IS WHY 'BEFORE EACH READ' IS NOT REDUNDANT. Read as a per-route rule, the contract would be satisfied by one `connection()` anywhere on the route — and every other read on it would be fresh, so nothing would look wrong. Then someone removes the compliant read, or moves it to a child route, or wraps it in a cached component, and every sibling silently reverts to build-time content. That is the exact failure mode DEC-0019 rejected `io()` for: correct until an unrelated change makes it quietly wrong. The per-read clause makes each read carry its own reason to be fresh, so the invariant survives refactoring. ⚠️ It also means TESTING CANNOT CATCH A VIOLATION on a compliant route — a non-compliant read passes every freshness check as long as a sibling is compliant. The enforcement has to be static (a rule about the code) rather than behavioural (a rule about the output), which is a real constraint on how the acceptance criteria at stage 7 can be written. ⚠️ Found only because the control was placed inside the same build rather than in a separate one.
statement: Under `next build` + `next start` with Next.js 16.3.2, a planning-content read that does not follow the DEC-0019 contract is nevertheless served fresh when another read on the same route does follow it, with cacheComponents both enabled and disabled — the compliant read makes the whole route dynamic and the non-compliant sibling rides along. The non-compliant read's freshness therefore depends on the continued presence of a compliant sibling on that route, and neither the build output nor the served page distinguishes a read that is fresh because it follows the contract from one that is fresh by proximity.
title: A non-compliant read is silently fresh while a compliant read shares its route

notes: ⚠️ THIS REFRAMES QST-0018 RATHER THAN ANSWERING IT. The question was posed as 'which components may a stage document execute', which presumes a permitted set exists to be configured. It does not. The component mapping is a substitution table for markdown elements and named components; it is not a gate, and nothing consults it before a document's own `import` runs. ⚠️ THE REAL QUESTION IS WHETHER THE AGENT IS A TRUSTED AUTHOR, and it is a product judgement rather than a research finding. MDX's own answer — trust the author or do not use MDX — puts the decision squarely on this project. #88 forbids hand-authoring artifacts precisely so the writer is a typed operation with a schema behind it; stage documents are the one agent-authored surface with no such check, and MDX would make them executable. That tension is the substance of this question and it is not resolved by more reading. ⚠️ SOURCE-SUPPORTED, NOT MEASURED. Every clause here is quoted from primary documentation. Nothing has been compiled or run, so this says what MDX is documented to do, not what this project's configuration was observed to do.
statement: Under the standard MDX toolchain a `.mdx` document compiles to a JavaScript module. It may contain arbitrary JavaScript expressions — the documentation states that expressions can contain whole JavaScript programs wrapped so they evaluate to something renderable — and it may use ESM `import` and `export` to reach any module the bundler can resolve. MDX provides no mechanism that restricts which components or modules a document may reference. Its documented security position is that MDX is a programming language whose safety rests on trusting the author, and that untrusted parties should not be permitted to author MDX.
title: An MDX stage document is a program, and MDX supplies no allowlist

derived.note: Derived at render time from the evidence graph (#96). Not stored on the artifact.

notes: ⚠️ THIS IS THE CANDIDATE ANSWER TO QST-0018'S THIRD PART, AND IT DOES NOT SURVIVE. The question asked what happens to a reference outside the permitted set — refuse, or render inert. MDX refuses, which sounds like the answer the question wanted. It is not: it refuses references to components that were never supplied, which is the case a mistaken author hits and not the case a capable one does. A document that reaches for something it should not have can simply import it, and then it IS defined. ⚠️ AND THE REFUSAL IS AT RUNTIME. Even used as a diagnostic, it surfaces when a page is rendered rather than when the document is written or the project is built — so a stage document with a bad reference is a page that throws for the operator, not a build that refuses. ⚠️ Same shape as AST-0022, one layer up: a mechanism that looks like enforcement because it produces an error, while the case it catches is not the case that matters.
statement: MDX requires a referenced component to be defined and fails at RUNTIME when it is not, with the message `Expected component X to be defined: you likely forgot to import, pass, or provide it`. The failure occurs when a reference resolves to nothing; a document that imports a component, defines one locally, or is passed one never reaches it. The check therefore reports an authoring mistake and does not constrain what a document may reference or execute.
title: MDX's missing-component error is a diagnostic, not a boundary

notes: ⚠️ THE THREE PROPERTIES ARE QUOTED; THE CONSEQUENCE BELOW IS AN INFERENCE FROM THEM, and it is flagged as one rather than presented as a fourth finding. If a per-page map MERGES WITH AND OVERRIDES the global map, then a page can add a component or replace one, and cannot take one away. So the mapping composes in the permissive direction only: there is no documented way to give one document a SMALLER set than another. Confirming that needs a compile, not another page. ⚠️ WHAT IT MEANS FOR THE COMPONENT BOUNDARY. A single global mapping is a reasonable place to state what stage documents may render, but it bounds only what is SUBSTITUTED — it is not consulted for a component the document imports itself (AST-0023). Treating it as the allowlist would be a boundary that is trivially bypassed by the one line an author is most likely to write.
statement: Using `@next/mdx` with the App Router requires an `mdx-components` file at the project root; the documentation states the integration will not work without it. The mapping it exports applies to all MDX files in the application rather than per document. Components passed to an individually imported MDX component merge with and override the global mapping.
title: In `@next/mdx` the component mapping is mandatory, global, and additive

notes: ⚠️ THE VULNERABLE LIBRARY IS NOT THE ONE THIS PROJECT WOULD USE, and saying so is the difference between evidence and alarm. `next-mdx-remote` compiles MDX at RUNTIME from a supplied string; `@next/mdx` compiles at BUILD time from files in the repository. The exposure is not the same and this CVE does not transfer directly. ⚠️ WHAT DOES TRANSFER IS THE MECHANISM. The vulnerability was not a bug in a parser — it is what AST-0023 already established, arriving as an incident: MDX expressions and ESM are code, so compiling a document IS executing its author's intent. `next-mdx-remote` was only the place that property met an untrusted author first. ⚠️ It answers the question this was held open for: whether anyone had run semi-trusted MDX and what went wrong. Someone did, and it was CWE-94.
statement: CVE-2026-0969 (GHSA-g4xw-jxrg-5f6m, GitHub-reviewed, high severity) records arbitrary code execution during React server-side rendering of untrusted MDX: the `serialize` function used to compile MDX in `next-mdx-remote` was vulnerable due to insufficient sanitisation of MDX content. Versions from 4.3.0 up to 6.0.0 are affected and 6.0.0 is the first patched release.
title: Server-side rendering of untrusted MDX is a demonstrated code-execution class, not a theoretical one

notes: ⚠️ THE REMEDY WAS SUBTRACTION, NOT FILTERING, and that is the most decision-relevant fact in this pass. The maintainers did not write a sanitiser that makes MDX safe; they removed the ability to run JavaScript and made removal the default. The one place they did attempt filtering, they labelled BEST EFFORT in their own documentation — a maintainer declining to call their own protection a boundary is worth more than any assurance they could have offered. ⚠️ IT ALSO ANSWERS THE SECOND THING THIS QUESTION WAS HELD OPEN FOR: whether restricting the compiler is something projects do or something that breaks in practice. It is now the DEFAULT behaviour of a mainstream library, and ESM removal ships as an off-the-shelf plugin. The restricted compile is the well-travelled path, not the bespoke one. ⚠️ Nothing here is measured against `@next/mdx`. Whether the same subtraction composes with a build-time bundler integration is a compile away and has not been run.
statement: `next-mdx-remote` 6.0.0 introduced `blockJS` and `blockDangerousJS`, both defaulting to true for security reasons, so JavaScript expressions in MDX are disabled by default from that release. With JS re-enabled, the remaining protection is described by its own maintainers as a best-effort option to block dangerous operations such as `eval`, `Function`, `process` and `require`; disabling it further is documented as safe only for content the operator completely trusts. Separately, removing `import` and `export` statements from MDX at compile time is available as a published remark plugin.
title: The ecosystem's remedy is to remove the capability at compile time, and its protective mode is best-effort

notes: ⚠️ BOTH BRANCHES ARE BAD, AND THE QUIET ONE IS WORSE. A package missing the narrative half of the plan is still a package: it validates, it renders, its MANIFEST reports counts that were never about stage documents, and nothing in it says nine files are absent. That is the well-formed false success this project keeps naming, arriving through a two-character change to a filename. ⚠️ THE OTHER BRANCH IS WHERE CVE-2026-0969 STOPS BEING SOMEONE ELSE'S INCIDENT. The package is the artefact this whole system exists to produce and hand to other people. Shipping executable author-controlled documents in it means the recipient's machine runs what the sending project's agent wrote — the same shape as the CVE, with the compile moved to their side of the handoff. ⚠️ It is a genuine argument for the restricted compile rather than against MDX. A document compiled with expressions and ESM removed is inert text plus a component vocabulary, and ships safely. The choice is not MDX-or-markdown; it is which MDX.
statement: The handoff publisher copies `planning-content/stages/*.md` verbatim into the published package, which currently carries nine stage documents. Because the filter matches only `.md`, converting stage documents to `.mdx` produces one of exactly two outcomes: with the filter unchanged, every stage document silently disappears from the package; with the filter widened, agent-authored documents that compile to JavaScript are shipped to whoever receives the package.
title: Making stage documents executable would export execution to package recipients — or silently drop them

statement: With `@next/mdx` on Next.js 16.3.2, a remark plugin calling `file.fail` on `mdxjsEsm`, `mdxFlowExpression`, `mdxTextExpression`, `mdxJsxExpressionAttribute`, object-valued `mdxJsxAttribute`, and JSX element names outside a permitted set causes `next build` to FAIL for each of those constructs, reporting the document path and a line:column position. notes: ⚠️ THIS REFUTES REQ-0018's SECOND CLAUSE FOR THE SUBSTRATE, by construction rather than by accident. The requirement asks that *a dropped update stream is visibly distinguishable from an idle one*. Byte-identical is the strongest possible form of indistinguishable — no client-side cleverness can recover a difference that was never transmitted. ⚠️ AND THE TWO GAPS COMPOUND. Per the WHATWG specification a client usually reconnects on its own (EVD-0054), which sounds like it makes the missed change harmless — it does not, because reconnection delivers nothing and the page only reloads on a message. So the page is stale, correctly connected, and silent, until some unrelated later change happens to arrive. ⚠️ Spec-side caveat carried explicitly: a FAILED connection is terminal and never retried (EVD-0051), and a non-200 or wrong Content-Type causes exactly that (EVD-0053). That path was not exercised here and is the one where the stream is genuinely gone for good. ⚠️ The server half is measured; browser reconnect behaviour is source-supported only.
statement: The walking skeleton's `/events` stream sends `retry: 500` once and then nothing until a change occurs: an idle stream emitted zero bytes over six seconds. It sends no `id:` field, so a reconnecting client has no `Last-Event-ID` to present and the server has no position to resume from; a change made while disconnected was not delivered after reconnection. A client therefore cannot distinguish an idle stream from a dead one, and cannot learn that it missed anything.
title: The skeleton's idle stream and its dead stream are byte-identical, and a gap is never recovered

statement: Per the WHATWG specification, a line in an event stream beginning with a colon is ignored by the client parser. notes: ⚠️ MEASURED IN HEADLESS CHROME, NOT REASONED ABOUT. In the page: `(() => { const t = { setTimeout }; try { t.setTimeout(()=>{},10) } catch (e) { return e.message } })()` returned `Illegal invocation`, while the same call wrapped as `(...a) => setTimeout(...a)` returned an id. Two `Illegal invocation` exceptions were recorded per page load. ⚠️ THE CONSEQUENCE IS SILENT BECAUSE THE THROW HAPPENS INSIDE AN EVENT LISTENER, which swallows it. The handler had already set the visible state before arming the timer, so the page showed its healthy state and simply never left it. ⚠️ NARROWED 2026-08-29, AND THE ORIGINAL WORDING IS WHY THIS NOTE EXISTS. It said the hazard was general — that `{ fetch }`, `{ addEventListener }` and `{ requestAnimationFrame }` 'all behave the same way'. NONE of those was measured. Two functions were. Reaching from one measured brand check to every browser global is the same move DEC-0020's fallback made about the compiler and the read span made about `lintProject`: a plausible cause stated with the confidence of an observed one, in an artifact whose whole purpose is to keep those apart. ⚠️ WHAT THE EVIDENCE DOES ESTABLISH: a receiver-sensitive browser function can fail when copied into a collaborator object and invoked as its method. Which functions are receiver-sensitive is a question this measurement does not answer. ⚠️ NO LINT RULE, BY PM DECISION. The default-path regression test in `test/stream-watchdog.test.mjs` protects the actual defect — it calls the shipped default with `globalThis.setTimeout` wrapped in a browser's brand check, and fails against the original code. A shared browser-adapter rule becomes worth building if a SECOND receiver-sensitive API is introduced, or if this defect recurs. Until then a rule would generalise from one instance, which is the error this note was written to record.
statement: A receiver-sensitive browser function can fail when copied into a collaborator object and later invoked as that object's method. MEASURED CASE: `const timers = { setTimeout, clearTimeout }` followed by `timers.setTimeout(fn, ms)` throws `TypeError: Illegal invocation`, because `Window.setTimeout`'s WebIDL brand check requires `this` to be the Window and the method call passes the containing object instead. Node applies no such check, so the identical code works there and every Node test of it passes. This claim covers `setTimeout` and `clearTimeout`; it does NOT assert that any other browser global behaves this way.

facts.browser: Google Chrome, headless=new, driven over CDP with no automation library

title: A receiver-sensitive browser function can fail when copied into a collaborator object
